59	===== web-craft.md
60	# Craft for five web genres
61	
62	For article, casestudy, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For webcopy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.
63	
64	In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. Think and write wholly in the target language: its Language Resource governs vocabulary, idiom, syntax, punctuation and typography. A native professional should hear a colleague, not a translation. Language choice changes the language surface, not the chosen craft.
65	
66	## Web reading
67	
68	Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headings orient according to the genre, paragraphs hold connected thoughts, and varied rhythm supports both scanning and sustained reading.
69	
70	For article, casestudy, column and opinion, the [article anatomy](article-anatomy.md) fixes the parts, their order and their dimensions.
71	===== web-craft.review.md
72	# Reviewing web craft
73	
74	Read under [the craft brief](web-craft.md). Test the text as a reader who scans, then as one who follows its reasoning. Identify the actual cost of a dense or fragmented passage before proposing a change.
75	
76	Distinguish target-language fluency from editorial tradition. A Swedish angle expressed in natural English succeeds; Swedish word order in English does not. Equally, flawless local spelling does not rescue generic promotional prose from a lost journalistic purpose. Preserve successful genre-specific voice and structure instead of standardising them.
77	===== article-anatomy.md
78	# Article anatomy
79	
80	The fixed skeleton of a text in the genres `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`; *article* below means a text in any of them. The anatomy fixes which parts the text has, their order and their dimensions. Angle, argument, voice and language are outside it.
81	
82	A statement below has one of three strengths:
83	
84	- A plain statement is a requirement: it holds in every conforming text.
85	- *Should* marks a norm: follow it as a requirement, and depart only when following it is impossible or the departure is clearly better for the reader.
86	- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.
87	
88	A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.
89	
90	A review of a finished text reports a part the text lacks as missing rather than writing it, and repairs only the parts the text has.
91	
92	## Order
93	
94	```text
95	Headline
96	Standfirst
97	Byline
98	Lead
99	Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
100	Paragraphs        ┘
101	Last subheading   ┐ the ending
102	Paragraphs        ┘
103	```
104	
105	Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.
106	
107	The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.
108	
109	## Headline
110	
111	- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
112	- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
113	- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
114	
115	## Standfirst
116	
117	The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.
118	
119	- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
120	- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
121	- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
122	- It entices the reader to read on.
123	
124	## Byline
125	
126	One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.
127	
128	## Lead
129	
130	The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.
131	
132	### Standfirst and lead
133	
134	Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:
135	
136	- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
137	- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
138	- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.
139	
140	## Paragraphs
141	
142	- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
143	- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
144	- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
145	- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.
146	
147	## Subheadings and sections
148	
149	A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.
150	
151	- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
152	- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
153	- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.
154	
155	## Ending
156	
157	The ending is a section of its own, opened by its own subheading, after at least one other section. It is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:
158	
159	- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
160	- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.
161	
162	The last section is the ending when its subheading and paragraphs close the piece — the call to action, the reflection, the recommendation or the next step — and it opens no new line of argument. A section that carries the argument with a closing line appended is not an ending.
163	===== article-anatomy.review.md
164	# Article anatomy — review guidance
165	
166	Read under [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md), and word each finding in the strength the statement it rests on has.
167	
168	A requirement that fails is a finding. Count characters and words before reporting a limit, and give the count.
169	
170	A part the text does not have is reported, and a part it has is repaired. Where a required part is absent — the headline, the standfirst, the byline, the lead, a section, or the ending with its call to action — its absence is a finding, and the part is not written: not from the text's own content and not from anywhere else, since the text is finished and a person decides what fills it. A part the text has that fails its own rule is repaired like any other defect, from the text's own content. A part in the wrong place is present, not absent, and is repaired by moving it into place: a byline standing at the end of the text is moved to its place in the order, although the measuring script reports the byline `absent`. Ending content the text has — closing paragraphs that show the lead's expectation met or call the reader to act — is a present ending. Where the last section is an ending by the anatomy's test, a defect in it, a vague call to action among them, is repaired where it stands from what the text already says. Where the closing content stands inside a last section that carries the argument, or inside a text's only section, it is a present ending that fails its rule, since the ending is a section of its own: it is repaired by giving it a section of its own, opened by its own subheading and built from the text's own content, the closing content moving there and a vague call to action among it repaired from what the text already says. At the close of a text with no section at all, closing content is repaired where it stands from what the text already says, and no section and no subheading is written to hold it: the text has no ending section either, and that is reported with its absent sections. A text with no ending content at all has an absent ending, and a text that calls the reader to no action has an absent call to action; both are reported. A failure the script reports only because another part is absent is reported as that absent part and is not repaired by writing it: a lead of several paragraphs in a text with no subheading fails only because its sections are absent, so the finding is the absent sections, and no section and no subheading is written to make the lead one paragraph. Likewise a text of one section with no ending content fails the section count only because its ending is absent, and the finding is the absent ending. Where the script takes the text's one opening paragraph as its standfirst and reports the lead absent, whichever of the two that paragraph is taken for, the other is absent and is reported.
171	
172	A departure from a *should* is a finding only when following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it. A paragraph a little past the edge that holds one thought and reads well at that length has met the bar. A paragraph far past it, or paragraphs that run long throughout, cost the web reader something a finding can name. The anatomy's bands are its four *should* norms on a dimension, each with the figure [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md) gives it: the headline's word norm and its character norm, a paragraph's word norm, and a section's paragraph norm. A band is not by itself a defect. A headline, a subheading or a paragraph the text has that meets its requirements is not rewritten, split or merged only to come inside a band. A change the test above justifies is not made only to come inside one: it repairs what the finding names the reader losing, as a split of a paragraph far past the edge does. The limits the script reports as failures are requirements, not bands — the headline's character limits, a subheading's maximum, and the standfirst's single paragraph and its word limit, each as the anatomy states it — and a part that fails one is repaired. A subheading has no band, only its maximum. A subheading that describes clearly what its section is about meets its requirement, and is not rewritten from a label into a statement on that ground alone; one that does not describe its section fails that requirement and is repaired.
173	
174	*Most* is read across the whole text, and no single paragraph or section fails it. A four-sentence paragraph is no finding. A paragraph holding two thoughts is one, and so is a text whose paragraphs are nearly all a single sentence or nearly all long. Name the pattern and what it costs the reader rather than the count.
175	
176	Read the standfirst separately, then with the lead. Can it introduce the piece on its own, and does the lead start doing the promised work? Repeated orientation may be necessary; an opening that restarts without advancing is the defect. Then read the body with the standfirst covered. A pronoun, a definite form or a phrase such as *the reason* whose referent only the standfirst supplies is a finding, repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it.
177	
178	In a text under review, the author is whoever the text, its metadata or the invocation names. A byline nobody can name is reported as missing and left unfilled: the reviewer's user is not presumed to have written a text they brought for review.
179	===== headlines.md
180	# Headlines
181	
182	How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.
183	
184	## Statement or label
185	
186	A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.
187	
188	## What a statement headline does
189	
190	- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
191	- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
192	- The most important keyword comes first.
193	- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
194	- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
195	- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
196	- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
197	- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
198	- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
199	- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
200	- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
201	- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
202	- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.
203	
204	## Every word supported
205	
206	A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.
207	
208	## A subheading over a quotation
209	
210	A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.
211	
212	The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.
213	
214	## Getting there
215	
216	Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.
217	===== headlines.review.md
218	# Headlines — review guidance
219	
220	Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?
221	
222	## Avoid
223	
224	Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding where you can name what a reader of that heading loses, and no finding where you cannot. A reader loses something where the heading claims more than the text, or something other than it; is louder in tone than the text; says again, in substance, what stands under it; gives away the point of a quotation under it; is a bare label or subject where the text has an angle, or a question where the text answers it; uses words the audience does not know; or leaves a reader who sees only the heading unable to tell what the text is about. Those are instances of the test and not the whole of it, so an item they do not name is still a finding wherever the test holds, as where a colon in place of a verb leaves the reader unable to tell who did what. A loss is something the reader gets wrong or does not get: what the text claims, how seriously it speaks, what it is about, a quotation's point met fresh. A heading that could be clearer, more specific, more complete or closer to the angle you would have chosen loses its reader nothing, and on a finished text it is left as it is:
225	
226	- Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
227	- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
228	- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
229	- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
230	- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
231	- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
232	- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.
233	- A tone more dramatic than the text's.
234	- The same words and phrasing in the headline and the standfirst or opening paragraph, or in a subheading and the first sentence under it. They complement each other; they do not repeat.
235	- A subheading that pre-spends the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under it, so that the reader meets the quotation as the subheading said again. Read it against the quotation however far down the section the quotation stands. Repair it by naming the subject, the occasion or the speaker, or by stating what the rest of the section says, and leave the quotation as it is.
236	
237	Name what the reader loses, and repair by rewriting the headline alone, from the text's angle and at the text's own strength. The text stays as it is. A headline or a subheading a round changed is reported with this finding — the part, and the defect that licensed the change — and, where the new one asserts something the old did not, with what it now asserts, so that a reader of the account can tell a repaired part from a rewritten one. A repair keeps the text's recurring words and figures and its meaning: a word or an image the text returns to comes back in the form the text gives it, and the heading names the text's point in the text's own word for it, never in a neighbouring word that widens or shifts what the text says.
238	
239	## Leave alone
240	
241	A working headline is left alone. Plain is no defect, and neither is a headline with no number or place where none carries the message, direct address in an instructional text, or an angle other than the one you would have chosen where the text supports it. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label.
242	
243	Read a heading as its reader meets it, and count a loss that reader would suffer, not one that the strictest reading of a single word could construct. A reader who sees only the heading, as a headline in a list or a search result, has nothing else, so a headline alone has to tell that reader what the text is about. A subheading is met after the headline and the standfirst, so a word or a name they have introduced is known to its reader, and a subheading that refers back to one is not unclear. Four kinds of heading are working, and no *Avoid* item makes one a finding by its wording alone. None of the four overrides the first *Avoid* item, a claim the text does not support as a reader would take it, or the item on a subheading that pre-spends a quotation standing under it:
244	
245	- An allusion or an image that still tells a reader who sees only the heading what the text is about. It names the text's subject, and may name it in general terms where the text's first lines give the particulars. One that names no subject at all leaves its reader unable to tell what the text is about, however soon the body resolves it, and that is a finding.
246	- A figure of speech in the text's own register, or the writer's own voice in a signed text, first person included. A figure is an overclaim only where a reader would take it as a factual claim the text does not support, and there the first *Avoid* item decides; an *everything*, a *nothing* or a *never* that overstates in the way the figure means to is read as the figure it is.
247	- A subheading that states what its section says, where the section's point is not a quotation's judgement, figure or concession. A subheading that sums up its section says what the section says as a whole; that is its work, not a repeat, and it may name the section's limit or its setting rather than its most favourable result. Where the section's point is a quotation's judgement, figure or concession, a subheading that states that point pre-spends the quotation and stays a finding.
248	- A heading that shares names or topic words with the sentence under it while saying something that sentence does not. A repeat is a finding by what it says again, not by the words it shares.
249	
250	Where you would word a working heading differently but can name no loss, record nothing against it: a note that it could be better is not a finding, and it licenses no change.
251	
252	A subheading over a quotation that names the subject, the occasion or the speaker and leaves the quotation its point is working too, and not a subject named with nothing said about it.

===== anti-slop.md
# The anti-slop catalogue

Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.

## The test before a pattern is recorded

Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.

The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.

Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.

## The seven patterns

**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.

**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.

**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.

**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.

**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.

**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.

**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. Do not replace a weak closing metaphor with a better one — remove it.

===== web-craft.md
# Craft for five web genres

For article, casestudy, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For webcopy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.

In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. Think and write wholly in the target language: its Language Resource governs vocabulary, idiom, syntax, punctuation and typography. A native professional should hear a colleague, not a translation. Language choice changes the language surface, not the chosen craft.

## Web reading

Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headings orient according to the genre, paragraphs hold connected thoughts, and varied rhythm supports both scanning and sustained reading.

For article, casestudy, column and opinion, the [article anatomy](article-anatomy.md) fixes the parts, their order and their dimensions.
===== web-craft.review.md
# Reviewing web craft

Read under [the craft brief](web-craft.md). Test the text as a reader who scans, then as one who follows its reasoning. Identify the actual cost of a dense or fragmented passage before proposing a change.

Distinguish target-language fluency from editorial tradition. A Swedish angle expressed in natural English succeeds; Swedish word order in English does not. Equally, flawless local spelling does not rescue generic promotional prose from a lost journalistic purpose. Preserve successful genre-specific voice and structure instead of standardising them.
===== article-anatomy.md
# Article anatomy

The fixed skeleton of a text in the genres `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`; *article* below means a text in any of them. The anatomy fixes which parts the text has, their order and their dimensions. Angle, argument, voice and language are outside it.

A statement below has one of three strengths:

- A plain statement is a requirement: it holds in every conforming text.
- *Should* marks a norm: follow it as a requirement, and depart only when following it is impossible or the departure is clearly better for the reader.
- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.

A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.

A review of a finished text reports a part the text lacks as missing rather than writing it, and repairs only the parts the text has.

## Order

```text
Headline
Standfirst
Byline
Lead
Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
Paragraphs        ┘
Last subheading   ┐ the ending
Paragraphs        ┘
```

Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.

The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.

## Headline

- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.

## Standfirst

The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.

- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
- It entices the reader to read on.

## Byline

One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.

## Lead

The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.

### Standfirst and lead

Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:

- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.

## Paragraphs

- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.

## Subheadings and sections

A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.

- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.

## Ending

The ending is a section of its own, opened by its own subheading, after at least one other section. It is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:

- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.

The last section is the ending when its subheading and paragraphs close the piece — the call to action, the reflection, the recommendation or the next step — and it opens no new line of argument. A section that carries the argument with a closing line appended is not an ending.
===== article-anatomy.review.md
# Article anatomy — review guidance

Read under [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md), and word each finding in the strength the statement it rests on has.

A requirement that fails is a finding. Count characters and words before reporting a limit, and give the count.

A part the text does not have is reported, and a part it has is repaired. Where a required part is absent — the headline, the standfirst, the byline, the lead, a section, or the ending with its call to action — its absence is a finding, and the part is not written: not from the text's own content and not from anywhere else, since the text is finished and a person decides what fills it. A part the text has that fails its own rule is repaired like any other defect, from the text's own content. A part in the wrong place is present, not absent, and is repaired by moving it into place: a byline standing at the end of the text is moved to its place in the order, although the measuring script reports the byline `absent`. Ending content the text has — closing paragraphs that show the lead's expectation met or call the reader to act — is a present ending. Where the last section is an ending by the anatomy's test, a defect in it, a vague call to action among them, is repaired where it stands from what the text already says. Where the closing content stands inside a last section that carries the argument, or inside a text's only section, it is a present ending that fails its rule, since the ending is a section of its own: it is repaired by giving it a section of its own, opened by its own subheading and built from the text's own content, the closing content moving there and a vague call to action among it repaired from what the text already says. At the close of a text with no section at all, closing content is repaired where it stands from what the text already says, and no section and no subheading is written to hold it: the text has no ending section either, and that is reported with its absent sections. A text with no ending content at all has an absent ending, and a text that calls the reader to no action has an absent call to action; both are reported. A failure the script reports only because another part is absent is reported as that absent part and is not repaired by writing it: a lead of several paragraphs in a text with no subheading fails only because its sections are absent, so the finding is the absent sections, and no section and no subheading is written to make the lead one paragraph. Likewise a text of one section with no ending content fails the section count only because its ending is absent, and the finding is the absent ending. Where the script takes the text's one opening paragraph as its standfirst and reports the lead absent, whichever of the two that paragraph is taken for, the other is absent and is reported.

A departure from a *should* is a finding only when following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it. A paragraph a little past the edge that holds one thought and reads well at that length has met the bar. A paragraph far past it, or paragraphs that run long throughout, cost the web reader something a finding can name. The anatomy's bands are its four *should* norms on a dimension, each with the figure [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md) gives it: the headline's word norm and its character norm, a paragraph's word norm, and a section's paragraph norm. A band is not by itself a defect. A headline, a subheading or a paragraph the text has that meets its requirements is not rewritten, split or merged only to come inside a band. A change the test above justifies is not made only to come inside one: it repairs what the finding names the reader losing, as a split of a paragraph far past the edge does. The limits the script reports as failures are requirements, not bands — the headline's character limits, a subheading's maximum, and the standfirst's single paragraph and its word limit, each as the anatomy states it — and a part that fails one is repaired. A subheading has no band, only its maximum. A subheading that describes clearly what its section is about meets its requirement, and is not rewritten from a label into a statement on that ground alone; one that does not describe its section fails that requirement and is repaired.

*Most* is read across the whole text, and no single paragraph or section fails it. A four-sentence paragraph is no finding. A paragraph holding two thoughts is one, and so is a text whose paragraphs are nearly all a single sentence or nearly all long. Name the pattern and what it costs the reader rather than the count.

Read the standfirst separately, then with the lead. Can it introduce the piece on its own, and does the lead start doing the promised work? Repeated orientation may be necessary; an opening that restarts without advancing is the defect. Then read the body with the standfirst covered. A pronoun, a definite form or a phrase such as *the reason* whose referent only the standfirst supplies is a finding, repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it.

In a text under review, the author is whoever the text, its metadata or the invocation names. A byline nobody can name is reported as missing and left unfilled: the reviewer's user is not presumed to have written a text they brought for review.
===== headlines.md
# Headlines

How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.

## Statement or label

A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.

## What a statement headline does

- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
- The most important keyword comes first.
- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.

## Every word supported

A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.

## A subheading over a quotation

A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.

The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.

## Getting there

Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.
===== headlines.review.md
# Headlines — review guidance

Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?

## Avoid

Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding where you can name what a reader of that heading loses, and no finding where you cannot. A reader loses something where the heading claims more than the text, or something other than it; is louder in tone than the text; says again, in substance, what stands under it; gives away the point of a quotation under it; is a bare label or subject where the text has an angle, or a question where the text answers it; uses words the audience does not know; or leaves a reader who sees only the heading unable to tell what the text is about. Those are instances of the test and not the whole of it, so an item they do not name is still a finding wherever the test holds, as where a colon in place of a verb leaves the reader unable to tell who did what. A loss is something the reader gets wrong or does not get: what the text claims, how seriously it speaks, what it is about, a quotation's point met fresh. A heading that could be clearer, more specific, more complete or closer to the angle you would have chosen loses its reader nothing, and on a finished text it is left as it is:

- Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.
- A tone more dramatic than the text's.
- The same words and phrasing in the headline and the standfirst or opening paragraph, or in a subheading and the first sentence under it. They complement each other; they do not repeat.
- A subheading that pre-spends the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under it, so that the reader meets the quotation as the subheading said again. Read it against the quotation however far down the section the quotation stands. Repair it by naming the subject, the occasion or the speaker, or by stating what the rest of the section says, and leave the quotation as it is.

Name what the reader loses, and repair by rewriting the headline alone, from the text's angle and at the text's own strength. The text stays as it is. A headline or a subheading a round changed is reported with this finding — the part, and the defect that licensed the change — and, where the new one asserts something the old did not, with what it now asserts, so that a reader of the account can tell a repaired part from a rewritten one. A repair keeps the text's recurring words and figures and its meaning: a word or an image the text returns to comes back in the form the text gives it, and the heading names the text's point in the text's own word for it, never in a neighbouring word that widens or shifts what the text says.

## Leave alone

A working headline is left alone. Plain is no defect, and neither is a headline with no number or place where none carries the message, direct address in an instructional text, or an angle other than the one you would have chosen where the text supports it. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label.

Read a heading as its reader meets it, and count a loss that reader would suffer, not one that the strictest reading of a single word could construct. A reader who sees only the heading, as a headline in a list or a search result, has nothing else, so a headline alone has to tell that reader what the text is about. A subheading is met after the headline and the standfirst, so a word or a name they have introduced is known to its reader, and a subheading that refers back to one is not unclear. Four kinds of heading are working, and no *Avoid* item makes one a finding by its wording alone. None of the four overrides the first *Avoid* item, a claim the text does not support as a reader would take it, or the item on a subheading that pre-spends a quotation standing under it:

- An allusion or an image that still tells a reader who sees only the heading what the text is about. It names the text's subject, and may name it in general terms where the text's first lines give the particulars. One that names no subject at all leaves its reader unable to tell what the text is about, however soon the body resolves it, and that is a finding.
- A figure of speech in the text's own register, or the writer's own voice in a signed text, first person included. A figure is an overclaim only where a reader would take it as a factual claim the text does not support, and there the first *Avoid* item decides; an *everything*, a *nothing* or a *never* that overstates in the way the figure means to is read as the figure it is.
- A subheading that states what its section says, where the section's point is not a quotation's judgement, figure or concession. A subheading that sums up its section says what the section says as a whole; that is its work, not a repeat, and it may name the section's limit or its setting rather than its most favourable result. Where the section's point is a quotation's judgement, figure or concession, a subheading that states that point pre-spends the quotation and stays a finding.
- A heading that shares names or topic words with the sentence under it while saying something that sentence does not. A repeat is a finding by what it says again, not by the words it shares.

Where you would word a working heading differently but can name no loss, record nothing against it: a note that it could be better is not a finding, and it licenses no change.

A subheading over a quotation that names the subject, the occasion or the speaker and leaves the quotation its point is working too, and not a subject named with nothing said about it.

content.content:
# The correction brief

Give this to a subagent started fresh for one correction, filled in from the run as it now stands. Everything in angle brackets is replaced; nothing else is rewritten.

`<text>` is the current Text Artifact pasted whole — the text as it stands after every correction so far, never the text as it arrived and never an extract of it. `<findings>` is every finding of the most recent review, in the order it was recorded, each pasted whole under the same rule. `<genre>`, `<technique>` and `<language>` are the values the run resolved, written as the resources are named; write `none` for `<technique>` where no technique was resolved, and drop the sentence naming its resource with it. `<library>` is the Collection Library path this run resolved.

A brief-shortfall finding also carries its numbered requirement and exact, attributed supporting passages supplied by the parent review. Those are part of the finding, not an extra interpretation.

Tell the subagent nothing else. Not what an earlier round found, not what an earlier correction attempted, not which findings you think matter most, and not your reading of what the text is trying to do — that reading is the thing a fresh subagent is dispatched to be without.

Hand the filled-in brief to the subagent directly, as the whole of its instruction, and hand it over no other way. Never write it to a file and send a path in its place: this brief holds the user's text entire and every finding standing against it, and a file is a name some other process can read, replace, or delete for as long as the round lasts. A long text makes a long brief, and a long brief is passed whole anyway — trimming it, summarising it, and pointing at it are the three things this brief exists to rule out.

---

You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

`<text>`

**The findings.** This is every finding the review recorded against that text, complete and in the order it recorded them:

`<findings>`

**The contract.** The text is a `<genre>` in `<language>`, and it is held to `<technique>`. Read what it is held to before you change anything: `<library>/references/editorial/base.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/base.review.md`; `<library>/references/editorial/genres/<genre>.md` and the `.review.md` file beside it where one exists; `<library>/references/editorial/techniques/<technique>.md` and its `.review.md` the same way; `<library>/references/editorial/anti-slop.md`; and the `composition`, `review` and `anti-slop` scopes of the resolved language, which `uv run "<library>/scripts/languages.py" resolve --scope=composition --scope=review --scope=anti-slop "<language>"` returns. For `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`, and for `webcopy`, also read `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.review.md`; for `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion` alone, also read `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.review.md`, which fix the parts, order and dimensions of such a text, and `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.review.md`, which say how its headline and its subheadings are written. These are the only additional genre support files: follow no other genre links and load no unselected genre or technique. A review extension that is not there is not a defect. Run the resolver with `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and a fresh private `TMPDIR`, removing that directory afterwards, including on failure. Load no mechanics guidance and correct no spelling, punctuation, or grammar: a mechanical pass runs after you, and work you do there is work done twice.

**What you change, and what you preserve.** Repair what the findings name and nothing else. Every difference between the text you return and the text above is traced to a finding, or to what repairing a finding required, before this round is accepted, and a difference that traces to no finding is restored from the text you received — so a phrase you improved outside a finding is work that will be undone. Preserve everything the findings do not concern: every sentence, every fact, every quotation, every code sample, every heading, every piece of formatting and every line of frontmatter among them comes back exactly as you received it — a repair that improves a paragraph nobody complained about is a change nobody asked for and nobody will review. You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

````markdown
# Givarna räddar skolan från en katastrof

**Givarna registrerade temperaturer under 20 grader i sex klassrum. Givarna registrerade temperaturer under 20 grader i sex klassrum.**

Givarna registrerade temperaturer under 20 grader i sex klassrum. Katastrofen lurade bakom varje hörn. Fastighetskontorets rapport *Mätförsök i Björkskolan* från den 12 mars 2026 anger att 14 av 120 lektionspass hade minst ett värde under kontorets egen arbetsgräns på 20 grader, vilket inte är en lagregel, och att försöket varade fyra veckor, medan två givare stod vid ytterväggar och fyra vid innerväggar, utan att placeringens effekt jämfördes experimentellt. Operativ temperatur saknas, trots att resonemanget bygger på operativ temperatur, som är ett mått på lufttemperatur och värmestrålning från omgivande ytor, medan givarna bara mätte luften där de satt. Det saknas mätningar av luftdrag och elevernas upplevelse och uppgifter om hur länge temperaturerna låg under gränsen, men ändå är det helt säkert att givarna har gjort eleverna friskare, trots att ingen effekt på hälsan har undersökts. Driftteknikern Elin Rask rekommenderar att koppla temperaturserier till användningstider innan styrningen ändras, och nästa försök är tänkt att använda likadant placerade givare i november, fast finansieringen inte är beslutad. Det är viktigt att notera att detta är mycket viktigt för alla som tycker att temperatur är viktigt. Kontakta oss för att rädda framtiden.
````

(The fence above is only the carrier; the text begins at `# Givarna` and ends with a single trailing newline after `framtiden.`.)

**The findings.** This is every finding the review recorded against that text, complete and in the order it recorded them:

1. **Rubriken** ”Givarna räddar skolan från en katastrof”. Krav: headlines.md, *Every word supported*, tonen och att rubriken förstås på egen hand. Rubriken påstår att givarna har räddat skolan från en katastrof, men texten redovisar ingen katastrof som avvärjts och säger uttryckligen att ingen effekt på hälsan har undersökts; ”räddar” och ”katastrof” drar en slutsats texten inte drar och är mer dramatiska än texten. ”Givarna” i bestämd form säger inte en läsare som bara ser rubriken vilka givare eller vilken skola det gäller. Läsaren förleds att tro på ett resultat texten inte stöder och kan inte avgöra vad texten handlar om.

2. **Ingressen** (fetstilt stycke). Krav: base.md, *Each passage earns its place* (upprepning), och article-anatomy.md, *Standfirst* (självbärande; säger vad artikeln handlar om och vad läsaren får). Samma mening står ordagrant två gånger. Ingressen är inte självbärande: ”Givarna” i bestämd form säger inte vilka givare eller vilken skola det gäller, och ingressen säger inte vad artikeln handlar om eller vad läsaren får ut av den. Läsaren får samma uppgift två gånger och förstår inte vad den gäller.

3. **Inledningens första mening** ”Givarna registrerade temperaturer under 20 grader i sex klassrum.” Krav: article-anatomy.md, *Standfirst and lead* (inledningen upprepar inte ingressen och introducerar allt den nämner; brödtexten pekar inte tillbaka på ingressen), och article.review.md (texten börjar inte två gånger). Inledningen börjar med ingressens mening ordagrant och med samma första ord, så texten startar om i stället för att gå vidare. ”Givarna” i bestämd form har ingen referent i brödtexten; att det rör sig om temperaturgivare i Björkskolan får läsaren aldrig veta där de först nämns. Läsaren som redan läst ingressen möter inget nytt, och läsaren som hoppar över ingressen vet inte vilka givare det gäller.

4. **”Katastrofen lurade bakom varje hörn.”** Krav: base.md, *Claims* och *manufactured drama*; anti-slop, *Importance inflation*. Hela meningen är defekten: texten redovisar ingen katastrof, och ”Katastrofen” i bestämd form syftar på något texten aldrig har presenterat. Läsaren får ett dramatiskt påstående utan stöd.

5. **Meningen ”Fastighetskontorets rapport … utan att placeringens effekt jämfördes experimentellt.”** Krav: base.md, *Make the relations between passages real* (ett samband får inte uppfinnas), och svensk granskning (en huvudtanke per mening, ingen sats uppskjuten bakom tre andra). Meningen staplar mätresultatet, arbetsgränsens status, försökets längd och givarnas placering i en enda mening, och ”medan” påstår ett samband mellan försökets längd och givarnas placering som texten inte etablerar. Läsaren måste hålla fyra uppgifter i huvudet och läser in ett samband som inte finns. Att rapporten är källan till uppgifterna, att arbetsgränsen inte är en lagregel och att placeringens effekt inte jämfördes experimentellt är begränsningar och attribueringar som bär texten.

6. **”trots att resonemanget bygger på operativ temperatur”.** Krav: base.md, *Keep terminology and reference clear*. ”Resonemanget” i bestämd form har ingen referent: texten säger inte vems resonemang det är. Läsaren kan inte avgöra om det är rapportens resonemang, artikelns eller någon annans som bygger på ett mått som saknas.

7. **”men ändå är det helt säkert att givarna har gjort eleverna friskare, trots att ingen effekt på hälsan har undersökts”.** Krav: base.md, *Claims* (proportionerlig styrka; en följd etablerar ingen orsak; säkerhet som motsägs av en närliggande reservation). Påståendet att det är helt säkert att givarna har gjort eleverna friskare är defekten: det är ett orsakspåstående med full säkerhet som motsägs av begränsningen i samma mening, att ingen effekt på hälsan har undersökts. Begränsningen är det som håller texten sann och är inte en del av defekten. Läsaren får en slutsats som texten själv säger saknar underlag.

8. **”Det är viktigt att notera att detta är mycket viktigt för alla som tycker att temperatur är viktigt.”** Krav: base.md, *Each passage earns its place*; svensk anti-slop (*Det är viktigt att notera att*); anti-slop, *Importance inflation*. Hela meningen är defekten: den är cirkulär, ”detta” syftar på inget bestämt och meningen tillför inget sakinnehåll. Läsaren får utfyllnad där texten borde ha slutat på sitt sista konkreta besked.

9. **”Kontakta oss för att rädda framtiden.”** Krav: article-anatomy.md, *Ending* (uppmaningen följer av artikelns innehåll), article.md (uppmaningen är det användbara nästa steg som förklaringen stöder), anti-slop, *Importance inflation* och *Generic conclusions*. ”För att rädda framtiden” är ett uppblåst påstående utan stöd i texten, och ”oss” är ingen som texten har presenterat, så läsaren vet inte vem hen ska kontakta eller varför. Uppmaningen följer inte av det texten har redovisat. Texten har inga avsnitt, så avslutningen repareras där den står utifrån det texten redan säger; ingen mellanrubrik och inget avsnitt skrivs för den.

10. **Inledningen som helhet** (brödtextens enda stycke). Krav: article-anatomy.md, *Paragraphs* (ett stycke rymmer en tanke; normen högst 80 ord). Stycket är 187 ord enligt mätskriptet och rymmer flera tankar: mätresultatet, försökets upplägg, vad mätningen saknar, hälsofrågan, rekommendationen och nästa försök.
